blocks.text: Atomic spectra provide evidence for quantised photons. The experimental arrangement consists of a discharge tube, a spectrometer and a diffraction grating (Fig 18.9): light from the source passes through a narrow slit and a collimator, which makes it parallel, falls on the grating, and is viewed through a rotating telescope. A series of bright lines is seen on a dark background. The vapours of different elements give different patterns of lines, called spectral series, which can be used to identify elements.

blocks.alt: Light from a discharge tube is focused by a lens on a narrow slit; the collimator makes it parallel and it falls on a diffraction grating at the centre of a table with a vernier angle scale. The diffracted colours enter a rotating telescope, viewed through its eyepiece.
blocks.caption: Figure 18.9: Spectrum produced with a diffracting grating (original drawing after the textbook's Figure 18.9).

blocks.title: Book correction
blocks.text: The printed Figure 18.9 labels the light source 'Beam of electrons'; the source is a discharge tube, as the text says and as drawn above.

One such series was identified by J. J. Balmer in 1885 in the spectrum of atomic hydrogen (Fig 18.10). In the visible region it has four lines, at 656 nm (red), 486 nm (blue-green), 434 nm (blue) and 410 nm (violet). J. R. Rydberg expressed the results in the formula 1/lambda = RH (1/2^2 - 1/n^2), where n = 3, 4, 5, ... is the excited energy level of the electron and RH = 1.0974 x 10^7 m^-1 is the Rydberg constant. The spectral lines of hydrogen also extend into the invisible ultraviolet and infrared regions. In the ultraviolet, the Lyman series is given by 1/lambda = RH (1/1^2 - 1/n^2), n = 2, 3, 4, ... (18.12). In the infrared, the Paschen series is given by 1/lambda = RH (1/3^2 - 1/n^2), n = 4, 5, 6, ... (18.13).

blocks.alt: A dark strip with coloured lines of hydrogen labelled 656 nm (red), 486 nm (blue-green), 434 nm (blue) and 410 nm (violet), and two more faint violet lines towards the UV end.
blocks.caption: Figure 18.10: Balmer series in the spectrum of atomic hydrogen (original drawing after the textbook's Figure 18.10).

blocks.alt: A vertical strip with wavelength increasing downwards. Red lines crowd at the top as the Lyman series (91 to 122 nm), then the Balmer series (365 to 656 nm), then the Paschen series from 820 nm downwards.
blocks.caption: For your information: Line spectrum of atomic hydrogen. Only the Balmer series lies in the visible region of the electromagnetic spectrum (original drawing after the textbook's For your information box).

blocks.text: These equations give the allowed energies of the electron in an isolated hydrogen atom (Figs 18.11 and 18.12). The state n = 1 is the ground state; n = 2, 3, 4, ... are excited states. An atom absorbs energy only in discrete amounts and is raised to one of its excited states. Excited states are very short-lived: the electron soon returns to a lower level, emitting a photon, and these photons form the emission spectrum of spectral lines. Transitions ending on n = 1 give the Lyman series, those ending on n = 2 the Balmer series, and those ending on n = 3 the Paschen series.

blocks.alt: Four horizontal lines with an Energy arrow pointing up: the ground state E0 (n = 1) at the bottom and the excited states E1 (n = 2), E2 (n = 3) and E3 (n = 4) above it.
blocks.caption: Figure 18.11: Energy levels (original drawing after the textbook's Figure 18.11).

blocks.alt: Hydrogen energy levels n = 1 to 7 and infinity on an Energy/10^-19 J axis (not to scale): -21.8, -5.45, -2.42, -1.36, -0.86 and 0.00. Arrows from n = 2, 3, 4, 5 to n = 1 are the Lyman series; from n = 3, 4, 5, 6 to n = 2 the Balmer series; from n = 4, 5, 6, 7 to n = 3 the Paschen series.
blocks.caption: Figure 18.12: Different transitions in the hydrogen atom (original drawing after the textbook's Figure 18.12).

blocks.title: Book correction
blocks.text: In the printed Figure 18.12 the third Balmer arrow starts again at n = 4; it starts at n = 5, as drawn above.

When light with a continuous spectrum, such as white light, passes through a gas at low pressure and is then analysed, light of certain wavelengths is found to be missing; dark lines appear in their places. This is an absorption spectrum. As the light passes through the gas, electrons absorb discrete amounts of energy and move to higher levels; only photons of certain energies are absorbed, exactly those needed for such upward transitions. When the excited electrons return to lower levels, photons of those same wavelengths are emitted, forming the emission spectrum. So the wavelengths missing from an absorption line spectrum are those present in the emission line spectrum of the same element (Fig 18.13).

blocks.title: Do you know?
blocks.text: To excite an atom, a photon must have energy exactly equal to the energy difference between two levels, hf = En - Ep. An electron striking the atom, however, can excite it if its kinetic energy is greater than or equal to that difference. The different types of spectra are continuous, line and band.

blocks.alt: Three strips on a 400 to 750 nm scale: (a) the continuous spectrum, a full band of colours from violet to red; (b) the hydrogen emission spectrum, bright lines at about 410, 434, 486 and 656 nm on black; (c) the hydrogen absorption spectrum, the colour band with dark lines at the same wavelengths.
blocks.caption: Figure 18.13: Relation between an absorption spectrum and the emission spectrum of the same element: (a) spectrum of white light, (b) emission spectrum of element, (c) absorption spectrum of the same element (original drawing after the textbook's Figure 18.13).
